def: A program that takes a program as input and produces the result of executing it.
A program that translates a program written in one language into an equivalent program in another language.
The language a compiler reads its input program in.
The language a compiler writes its output program in.
Translating code before it runs, commonly to machine code.
A compact instruction set for a software execution environment, which may interpret it or compile it to machine code.
A software execution environment for an instruction set, which may interpret instructions or compile them to machine code.
Compiling parts of a program to machine code while the program is running, usually the parts that run most often.
The part of a compiler that reads source text, checks it, and builds an internal representation of the program.
The part of a compiler that improves the program in an internal form, usually largely independent of the source language and target machine.
A data structure or language a compiler uses to hold the program between reading the source and writing the target.
The part of a compiler that turns the intermediate representation into instructions for one particular target machine.
A small, very fast storage slot inside the processor that instructions read and write directly.
A text form of machine instructions that maps almost directly onto the bytes the processor runs.
A program that turns assembly language text into machine code.
A file containing machine code and linking information, not yet combined with the other pieces it needs to run.
A program that combines object files and libraries into an executable or library, connecting references between them.
A command that coordinates compilation and linking, and separate assembly when needed, on your behalf.
Generating code that keeps every intermediate result on a stack, pushing operands and popping them when an operation needs them.
Building a compiler using an earlier compiler, so that a language's compiler can eventually be built from itself.
A compiler written in the same language it compiles.
The address of the instruction just after a call, saved on the stack so the callee's ret can resume the caller there.
The set of rules that says how functions pass arguments, return results, and share registers and the stack.
The register that holds the address of the next instruction the processor will execute, called %rip on x86-64.
A register that ordinary instructions can use for any integer or address value.
Storing a multi-byte value with its least significant byte at the lowest address.
A register whose status bits record facts about arithmetic or compare results, such as whether they were zero or negative.
The assembly syntax GNU tools use by default, with the source operand first and size suffixes on many mnemonics.
An instruction operand that names a location in memory by computing its address from registers and a constant.
A jump that changes %rip only if its condition holds, usually a test of flag bits, and otherwise falls through to the next instruction.
A region of ordinary memory that functions use for return addresses, saved registers and local variables, growing and shrinking as calls happen.
The register %rsp, which holds the address of the current top of the machine stack.
The block of stack memory one function call owns, holding its saved registers and local variables.
The instructions at the start of a function that set up its stack frame.
A register, usually %rbp, that holds a fixed address inside the current frame so locals can be found at constant offsets from it.
The instructions at the end of a function that tear down its stack frame and return.
The 128 bytes below %rsp that System V guarantees no signal handler will overwrite, usable by a function as scratch space.
Application binary interface, the rules compiled code must follow to interoperate, including the calling convention and data layout.
The registers a calling convention assigns to pass a function's first arguments.
A register a called function may use only if it restores the original value before returning.
A register a called function may overwrite freely, so a caller that needs its value after the call must save it first.
The rule that %rsp must be a multiple of some size, 16 bytes here, at a particular point in a call.
A tool that turns machine code bytes back into assembly text.
A word the language reserves for its own syntax, which therefore cannot be used as a name.
One meaningful unit of source text, represented here by its category together with the text it came from.
The category a token belongs to, such as identifier, integer literal or less-or-equal operator.
The exact characters from the source that make up one token.
The compiler phase that reads source characters and produces a stream of tokens, also called a scanner.
The lexing rule that the next token is always the longest prefix of the remaining input that forms a valid token, also called longest match.
Go's lexer rule that adds a semicolon token at the end of a line when the line's last token is one of the kinds listed by the specification.
A pattern that describes a set of strings using concatenation, alternation and repetition.
The regular expression operation that matches anything either of two patterns matches.
The regular expression operation that matches zero or more repetitions of a pattern.
A set of strings that some regular expression describes.
A finite automaton that may have several transitions for the same character from one state, and that accepts a string if some way of following its arrows while reading it ends in an accepting state.
A transition that a machine may follow at any time without reading an input character.
A method that builds an NFA from a regular expression by combining one small NFA fragment per operator.
A finite automaton in which every state has at most one transition for each input character, so the next state is never in doubt.
The set of NFA states reachable from a given set by ε-transitions alone, including the set itself.
The algorithm that builds a DFA whose states are the sets of NFA states reachable on some input.
Merging the states of a DFA that no input string can tell apart, giving the smallest equivalent DFA.
A tool that reads token rules written as regular expressions with actions and writes the source code of a lexer.
Widening a value to more bits by filling the new high bits with zeros.
One situation a machine can be in, standing for everything it needs to remember about the characters read so far.
A rule that moves a machine from one state to another when the next input character is a given one, drawn as a labelled arrow.
A state meaning that the characters read so far form a complete string the machine recognises, drawn as a double circle.
A machine with a fixed set of states, a start state, accepting states and labelled transitions, which reads its input one character at a time.
The compiler phase that reads the token stream and builds the tree that shows how the tokens group into phrases.
A set of rewriting rules, each replacing one named kind of phrase by a sequence of tokens and phrase names, together with a starting phrase name.
A grammar symbol that stands for a token kind and is never rewritten.
A grammar symbol that names a kind of phrase and is rewritten by the grammar's rules.
One grammar rule, saying that the nonterminal on its left may be replaced by the sequence of symbols on its right.
The nonterminal every derivation of a whole program begins from.
A sequence of strings that starts with the start symbol and turns each string into the next by rewriting one nonterminal with one of its productions.
A derivation that rewrites the leftmost nonterminal at each step.
A tree whose inner nodes are nonterminals, each with the right side of the production that rewrote it as its children, and whose leaves are tokens (or ε for an empty production).
Extended Backus-Naur Form, a grammar notation that adds optional parts and repetition to plain productions.
Backus-Naur Form, the plain notation for context-free productions.
A grammar under which some sentence has more than one leftmost derivation, or equivalently more than one parse tree.
The ambiguity in which an else after two nested ifs could belong to either one.
The rule that decides which of two different operators takes its operands first, as when multiplication groups before subtraction.
The rule that decides how a run of operators of equal precedence groups, from the left or from the right.
A parser that builds the tree from the root downward, choosing each node's production before reading the tokens that production covers.
A nonterminal deriving, in one or more steps, a sequence beginning with itself, directly or through other rules.
The next unread token, which the parser examines to choose a production.
For a grammar symbol or sequence, the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from it, plus ε if it can derive the empty string.
A state that one more round of a repeated update leaves unchanged.
For a nonterminal, the set of terminals, plus eof, that can appear immediately after a string derived from it.
For a production, the FIRST set of its right side without ε, plus the FOLLOW set of its left side if the right side can be empty.
A grammar in which, for every nonterminal, the START sets of its alternatives do not overlap.
Parsed by scanning the input Left to right, building a Leftmost derivation, with 1 token of lookahead.
A parsing method built from one procedure per nonterminal, each recognising its nonterminal and calling the others for the nonterminals in its productions.
Parsing expressions with one loop that compares the binding power of each operator it meets against a minimum passed down by its caller.
A number saying how tightly an operator holds its operands, so that a higher number groups first.
Parsing expressions by a loop that absorbs operators whose precedence is at least a minimum and parses each right operand with a minimum chosen for its associativity.
